summary: Recommends that the control word always be used with Ethernet pseudowires. RFC 4448 made it optional, and without it an Ethernet packet can be mistaken for IP by a label switching router, possibly causing the wrong load-balancing path to be chosen.

eli5.summary: A package without a label may be mistaken for something else and sent the wrong way. Adding the label stops that.

subtitle: Why Ethernet pseudowires should almost always carry the control word, so routers stop mistaking Ethernet frames for IP packets.

tldr.problem: Without the control word, an Ethernet pseudowire packet can be mistaken for an IP packet by a label switching router, which may then pick the wrong equal-cost multipath path and misorder packets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC updates RFC 4448 so that both provider edges SHOULD support the Ethernet pseudowire control word and, if supported, MUST use it.
tldr.outcome: The control word removes the ambiguity between Ethernet pseudowire and IP payloads, so the use of the control word is recommended in all but exceptional circumstances.

today: RFC 8469 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4448, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the reference for using the Ethernet pseudowire control word.

sections.title: The Misidentification Problem
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries Ethernet over an MPLS network. RFC 4448 made the control word (CW) optional for Ethernet pseudowires. This RFC explains why that choice causes trouble.

Many label switching routers (LSRs) look past the end of the label stack to decide whether the payload is an IP packet. If it is, they choose the next hop from the so-called five-tuple: IP source address, IP destination address, protocol/next-header, and transport-layer source and destination ports.

Without a CW, an Ethernet PW packet can be misidentified as IP. An LSR that picks an equal-cost multipath (ECMP) path this way may send the packet down the wrong path, which can misorder packets. Flow misordering can also happen on a single path when traffic classification and differential forwarding treatment are in use.
sections.eli5: Some routers peek inside a package to guess what it is. If they guess wrong, they send it down a different road than its friends, and the packages arrive in the wrong order.

sections.title: Why the Problem Got Worse
sections.content:
IPv4 and IPv6 packets start with the values 0x4 and 0x6. An Ethernet PW packet without a CW can look like IP if the Ethernet destination address starts with either value.

When pseudowires were first deployed, some commercially significant equipment could not process the Ethernet CW. It was also believed that no Ethernet MAC address had been issued by the IEEE Registration Authority Committee (RAC) starting with 0x4 or 0x6, so skipping the CW seemed safe.

That assumption no longer holds. The RAC has since issued MAC addresses starting with 0x4 or 0x6, and equipment using them has been deployed. Privacy-driven MAC address randomization also assigns local addresses at random, which gives a start of one of these two values approximately one time in eight.

Some vendors responded with more complex, proprietary heuristics that inspect transit packets. The RFC says these cannot be reliable because of the random nature of the payload. A posting on the NANOG email list highlighted the problem.
sections.eli5: People once thought no one used addresses that looked like the confusing kind. Later those addresses were handed out, and phones that pick random addresses make the mix-up happen often.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
Using the Ethernet PW CW resolves the ambiguity between an MPLS payload that is an Ethernet PW and one that is an IP packet. The RFC updates RFC 4448 to say that both the ingress and the egress provider edge (PE) SHOULD support the Ethernet PW CW, and that if it is supported, the CW MUST be used.

The abstract puts it as a recommendation to use the CW in all but exceptional circumstances. The CW, defined for PWs in RFC 4385, also provides sequencing of individual frames, avoidance of ECMP and OAM mechanisms, as quoted from RFC 4448.

Implementations still have to be able to send and receive frames without the CW, as RFC 4448 required for backwards compatibility with early deployments.
sections.eli5: The rule is simple: put the label on every package whenever you can, and if you have the labels, always use them.

sections.title: Load Balancing with ECMP
sections.content:
When an Ethernet PW carries enough traffic that ECMP is required, one of two methods may be used. RFC 6391 (Flow-Aware Transport of Pseudowires, FAT PW) increases the entropy of the bottom-of-stack label and needs both PEs to support it. RFC 6790 (entropy labels) puts an entropy value in the LSP part of the label stack, and needs both PEs to insert and remove the entropy label (EL) and its indicator (ELI).

If both PEs support both methods, either may be used. Using both on the same PW is not normally necessary and should be avoided unless circumstances require it. For multi-segment PWs, ELI/EL SHOULD be used on every segment, but how that is guaranteed is out of scope.

The PW label is pushed first, then the LSP label. The ELI/EL labels belong to the LSP layer, so they are pushed after the PW label.

OAM packets are easier to keep on the same path as data with either method than when ECMP is based on the five-tuple of an IP payload, for which no method is currently known.
sections.eli5: If one road is too busy, you can add a tag to each package that tells the sorting machines which road to use, so packages from the same family stay together.

sections.title: Mitigations and Operational Notes
sections.content:
Where the CW cannot be used, the effects of ECMP can be avoided by carrying the PW over a traffic-engineered path that does not load-balance the payload, such as one set up with RSVP-TE (RFC 3209). The downsides are that such paths may still face link-bundle load balancing, and the single LSP has to carry the full PW load.

In some equipment, whether a CW is included depends on configuration, and the default may disable it. Software implementing this recommendation must not depend on existing settings that prevent use of a CW. The RFC recommends that platform software emit a rate-limited message saying the CW can be used but is disabled by configuration.

MPLS has no payload type in the packet. It relies on the control plane to signal what follows the label stack. Some LSRs deduce the type by inspecting the payload, sometimes past the PW CW. That is not an exact science, and operators who enable it should know that frames may still arrive out of order despite the CW. Such misordering can be hard to diagnose.
sections.eli5: If you cannot add the label, you can send everything down one dedicated road, but then that one road has to carry everything. Equipment should also warn people when a label switch is turned off.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC expresses a preference for one existing, widely deployed Ethernet PW encapsulation over another. The two have identical security considerations, which RFC 4448 discusses, so no additional security issues are introduced. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Choosing the labeled package over the unlabeled one is no riskier, so nothing new needs guarding.
